title: Fellowship (Acts 2:42)
hook: the first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayers
carry: you weren't meant to do it alone

segments.voice: Yesterday: gospel, Taizé and the worship band, three rooms praying in three sounds. Your line was every style can pray. Did you listen to something new? A new week starts now: together and alone. Day one hundred forty.
screen: `EVERY STYLE CAN PRAY.` → `A NEW WEEK: TOGETHER AND ALONE.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem, a few weeks after Easter. Something has happened at Pentecost, and suddenly there are thousands of new believers where there were about a hundred and twenty. No church buildings. No clergy training. No plan. What do they actually do, day to day? The book of Acts gives a snapshot, and it's surprisingly ordinary. They listen to the apostles teach. They eat together in each other's homes. They pray. They share what they have, so nobody goes without. It reads less like the founding of a religion and more like a very large family learning to live together. And tucked in the middle of that list is a Greek word the church has never stopped using. Today's word.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF NEW BELIEVERS.` → `NO BUILDINGS, NO PLAN.` → `THEY ATE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Koinonia. It comes from koinos, common, shared, what belongs to everyone. So koinonia is having something in common: partnership, participation, sharing. English usually translates it fellowship, which is fine, but it's thicker than coffee after church. Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Four things. Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayers. Churches still use that verse as a checklist. Now watch how the same word gets used elsewhere in the New Testament. Paul uses koinonia for money: a collection the churches took up for poor believers in Jerusalem. Sharing your wallet is koinonia. He uses it for the bread and cup: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" That word communion is koinonia. And he uses it for sharing in someone's suffering. So one word covers a meal, a bank transfer, the Lord's Supper and a hard season. That tells you what the first Christians thought church was. Not an event you attend. A life you share. Acts says they ate their meals with gladness. There's a line in Genesis, right at the start, that sits underneath all this: "It is not good that the man should be alone." Christians have many ways of living it out. Some churches keep a meal after every service. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of the whole church, living and dead, sharing one communion. Many Protestants meet in homes midweek. Different forms, one conviction: faith was never meant to be carried solo.
screen: `KOINOS — COMMON, SHARED.` · `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYERS.` · `A MEAL, MONEY, THE CUP, SUFFERING.` · `A LIFE YOU SHARE.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT GOOD THAT THE MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Picture the last meal you shared with someone, really shared, not just ate near. Where were you? What did you talk about? Now let a face come to mind: someone you haven't eaten with in too long. A friend, a neighbor, a parent, someone who might be lonelier than they let on. Hold that face for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just wish them well. Then decide: a meal, a coffee, even a sandwich on a bench, this week. The bell holds the time.
Koinonia. Greek for sharing a common life. Fellowship, communion, partnership: a meal, a purse and a faith held together.
Your line: you weren't meant to do it alone. Today, share a meal with someone, or set a date to. Day one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Many churches keep fellowship through shared meals, coffee after services, home groups and collections for people in need, and many Christians take Acts 2:42 as a picture of what church life should include.

myth: koinonia just means socializing after church
it means sharing a common life: meals, money, the Lord's Supper and suffering.
Paul used the same word for a money collection and for communion
koinonia covers both: sharing your wallet and sharing the cup.
koinonia comes from a Greek word meaning holy
it comes from koinos: common, shared, what belongs to everyone.

fork.setup: you're one of thousands of new believers in Jerusalem. there are no buildings, no clergy, no plan. what do you do?
options: wait for leaders to organize something.
listen to the apostles, eat together, pray and share.
fork.reveal: they continued in teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers, eating together in homes with gladness, sharing so nobody went without.

original.note: Greek: sharing, partnership, communion — from koinos, common.

trapdoor: what you thought: fellowship means a potluck in the church basement.
what it means: sharing a common life: the table, the purse, the prayers and the hard seasons.
what a scholar hears: koinonia, used by Paul for a money collection, for participation in Christ's body and blood, and for sharing in suffering.

sources.quoted: And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.

notes: Uses of koinonia: Romans 15:26 (a contribution for the poor in Jerusalem), 1 Corinthians 10:16 (communion), Philippians 3:10 (fellowship of his sufferings). Confirm.
'Barely a hundred' before Pentecost: Acts 1:15 gives about 120; Acts 2:41 about 3,000 added. Confirm phrasing.
Orthodox and Catholic teaching on the communion of saints stated briefly; confirm.

Audit (10% sample): hook's 'barely a hundred' corrected to 'about a hundred and twenty' (Acts 1:15); replaced the myth 'the first believers met mostly in church buildings', which repeated day 20's myth and angle almost word for word, with one about the root koinos.
